A society flourishes when it operates at maximum power, and that maximum flow of energy requires a good gradient between plenitude and suffering. There has to be more people wanting than there are having.

We need something to run from. It seems like there is an idea in certain ethics, maybe the Rawlsian equality sort, where if it were the case that every choice we made in life, every action we took, could at worst result in still being fed and sheltered (i.e. some universal line of worst outcome), that this would cause people to take more risk. That this would facilitate the greatest creative efforts and the most liberated kinds of "reaching" would flower. I disagree. I think a parachute does the opposite.

Though, I don't have the answer for exactly what the number would look like. Obviously, there is a level of depravity where things become runaway, and ubiquitous suffering cannot catapult people into useful striving when there is no opportunity. The suffering we saw in certain socialist systems is a good example. It seems like there is, theoretically anyway, some optimum distribution of resources and opportunity that would facilitate a society's maximum power (note, not the power of any one person or group of individuals, but the maximum power of the group). I only argue that there cannot be equilibrium. There must always be inequity in power. It's why society forms to begin with. People gathered in the city because something was there to be had, something they didn't have. If not for that being the case, then the only draw to such a cramped place would be vice. So the concept of opportunity and a means to have a realistic shot at participating in the game are both necessary. How that would look statistically, I don't know. What is the optimum distribution of a wealthy class? I don't know. At what point does the growth of poverty within a society become too much for the society to sustain?

I don't know. But I believe we ought to look at societies themselves like living organisms. A gradient from plenitude to poverty in a society is something I'd say is requisite. There has to be winners and losers. The game has to be risky enough that it is worth it to play, but not so risky that there are too many losers. A society cannot tolerate poverty over a certain threshold. Neither can it tolerate wealth that is too concentrated in the hands of too few.
